title: Coffee-run relay
start: A four-slot carrier tray of moulded ivory card, about the width of a paperback, sits at the front left of a pale neutral tabletop. One slot holds a tall ivory paper cup with a frosted acrylic lid, and a thin curl of steam rises from its sip hole. A crisp acid-lime paper sleeve wraps that cup, marking the one order that matters. The other three slots are empty, their pressed fibre walls showing faint mould seams. To the right, a brushed graphite pickup shelf holds a blank ivory order slip under a small graphite bulldog clip. Behind it, a short stack of unused trays waits, nested neatly. A few loose fibres and one faint ring of condensation mark the tabletop. Everything is square, still and on time.
end: The same carrier tray is now the base of a leaning tower of nested trays a dozen high, every slot filled with an ivory cup, the frosted lids fogged and no steam left anywhere. The tower sways to the right, frozen mid-lean. The top two trays are sliding free and three cups are tipping out, lids popping off and pale milky coffee arcing through the air in thick droplets. The original cup with the acid-lime sleeve is trapped at the very bottom, slightly crushed, its sleeve creased. Blank order slips have piled on the graphite pickup shelf until it bows in the middle. Spilled milky liquid runs across the tabletop toward the front edge, soaking the tray bottoms dark and soft. Cold condensation beads on every cup.
apocalypse: A wide, flat delta of dried pale milky sediment spreads to a low horizon, cut by shallow braided channels that still hold thin films of liquid. At its head stands the collapsed tower of carrier trays, now the size of a tenement block, its ivory card walls bleached, sagging and split along the moulded seams. Toppled cups the height of grain silos lie half sunk in the silt, their frosted lids cracked and scattered like fallen roof domes. The graphite pickup shelf juts from a channel bank as a pitted, bowed pier. In the foreground, a slim graphite cable crane on three splayed legs lowers an acid-lime cradle around one intact cup and lifts it clear of the mud. Fine dust lines every ridge, and tide rings circle the ruins.

title: Autopilot remote
start: A slim handheld remote, about the length of a pencil, lies diagonally at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its body is brushed graphite metal with chamfered edges, two small screws on the back plate and a grid of blank frosted acrylic buttons. One oval button near the top is acid-lime, slightly worn at its centre from use. To its left stands a tear-off desk calendar on a graphite easel base: a thick block of blank ivory paper pages bound under a graphite clip. Behind the calendar sit a cold frosted glass mug and a folded ivory card note, left by someone who stepped out. Only the top calendar page lifts slightly, curling at one corner. Light dust rests along the remote's seams.
end: The same remote now lies with its acid-lime button pressed flat, held down by the folded card note, which has slipped onto it. The tear-off calendar is shedding pages in a continuous stream: dozens of blank ivory sheets are frozen mid-air, fanning out to the left in a long arc like a riffled deck, the nearest sharp and the farthest smeared with motion. The calendar block has shrunk to a thin sliver under its clip. The desk around it has aged in the same moment. The frosted mug is clouded with a ring of dried residue, the tabletop is furred with dust, and the pages already lying at the edge are yellowed and brittle, curling at the corners. The paper stream traces straight back to the clip.
apocalypse: A grey-ivory basin of drifted paper stretches away under still, dusty air, the drifts layered like old snow and the lowest sheets pressed into brittle beige strata. Near the middle rises the calendar easel, now the size of a radio mast, its graphite clip jaws open and empty, one leg buckled. The remote lies half buried nearby like a fallen bridge span, its frosted buttons clouded and cracked, the back plate lifted at one corner around a stripped screw. A frosted glass mug as big as a water tower sits tilted and filled with dust. In the foreground, a low graphite tracked rig extends a long boom and presses an acid-lime pad onto the remote's worn pause button, and the nearest drift has stopped creeping, its leading edge frozen.

title: Say yes to everything
start: A shallow inbox tray of brushed graphite, about the size of a letter sheet, sits front centre on a pale neutral tabletop, holding one ivory request slip with a neatly folded corner. To its right stands a spring-loaded desk stamp: a graphite handle, a chamfered column and a square rubber face inked in acid-lime, poised above an empty blotter of ivory card. The spring is visible through a frosted acrylic sleeve on the column. Behind them sits a graphite outbox tray, still empty and waiting. A cold frosted mug sits at the back right corner. Fine fibres lift from the slip's deckled edge, and a thin film of dust rests on the blotter. The desk is tidy, and the flow is one slip in, one slip out.
end: The same stamp is frozen at the bottom of a hard stroke, its spring fully compressed, and every slip in reach now carries its acid-lime ink square. Slips pour out of the inbox tray, which has overflowed into a heap, and a blizzard of stamped ivory slips is frozen mid-air, arcing up and to the right over the outbox tray, now buried in a drift. Some slips carry two or three overlapping squares. The ivory blotter is soaked through with ink and curling at its corners. A fan of slips has slid off the far edge of the table, and a few have landed across the cold mug. A trail of tiny ink droplets and bent slip corners runs straight back to the stamp face.
apocalypse: A frozen avalanche of ivory slips has swept down a long valley, burying a grid of low graphite blocks that read as a city seen from far above; only rooftops and a few chamfered towers break the surface. Every slip is faded, the old ink squares bleached to a dull pale grey. At the head of the valley the stamp lies on its side, now as big as a cathedral, its spring snapped and uncoiled across the paper snow, its handle cracked through. Across the valley mouth stands a slim graphite sorting gate on stilts with an acid-lime sieve screen. The slips pile against it, and only a thin trickle passes through into a neat graphite channel below, stacking into a short, orderly pile. Dust hangs in the valley air.

title: Stopwatch logistics
start: A short sorting belt of matte graphite rollers, about a forearm long, runs left to right across a pale neutral tabletop. On it sits one ivory card parcel the size of a matchbox, tied with ivory string, a blank label on top. Strapped to its side with a thin graphite band is a small graphite stopwatch with a plain dial with tick marks and a single acid-lime second hand, frozen just short of the top. At the right end of the belt waits an empty frosted acrylic chute. Behind the belt lie a few flat, unfolded parcel blanks, crisp and unused. Fine card dust has collected between the rollers, and the string's loose fibres catch the light.
end: The same belt is now crowded end to end with parcels, each strapped to its own graphite stopwatch, the hands all at different angles. The rollers have sped up into a blur, and parcels are frozen mid-flight off the right end, spinning over the frosted chute, which is jammed and overflowing. Two parcels have burst open in the air, releasing crumpled ivory packing paper. The flat blanks behind the belt have been folded up and forced onto it, crushing at their corners. The first parcel, its acid-lime second hand still visible, is caught mid-tumble at the front of the arc, its strap snapped. A trail of stopwatch lids, snapped string and card scraps leads back along the belt to where it began.
apocalypse: A wide, empty beach of pale ivory sand curves to a flat grey horizon, low waves frozen as thin frosted ridges along the shore. Along the tide line lie washed-up parcels the size of houses, their card walls swollen, delaminated and bleached, string strands thick as ship rope trailing into the water. The graphite sorting belt emerges from the dunes behind as a long broken pier, its rollers seized and half missing. A giant stopwatch lies face up in the shallows, its frosted crystal cracked and filled with sand, its dial blank. In the foreground, a slim graphite outrigger raft with an acid-lime mast has winched one small intact parcel aboard with a thin graphite davit and points out across the calm water toward the horizon.

title: Door vault conveyor
start: A tall graphite storage rack, about the height of a wine bottle, stands at the right of a pale neutral tabletop, divided into narrow vertical slots like a plate rack. A thin graphite floor rail runs from the left edge into its base. Six slots hold miniature plain doors: flat ivory card panels with bevelled edges and small graphite knobs, each in a slim graphite frame. On the rail, one more framed door is sliding into the next empty slot, a tiny acid-lime latch on its frame about to click home. Two slots remain empty. A few card fibres and a fine line of metal dust sit in the rail's groove. The rack is plumb and evenly spaced.
end: The same rack is being overfed. Framed doors crowd the floor rail nose to tail, pushed in faster than the rack can take them. The door with the acid-lime latch has missed its slot and wedged diagonally across two, its frame bent. Behind it the rail has buckled upward, and a pile-up of doors is frozen mid-collision: several have swung open in their frames, two knobs have popped loose and hang airborne, and one door is falling off the rail toward the viewer. Inside the rack, doors have been shoved sideways and lean against each other like toppled dominoes. Card panels crease at their hinges, and bright metal shavings glint along the buckle, all tracing back to the jammed slot.
apocalypse: A broad canyon floor runs between two sheer walls built from stacked, bleached ivory door panels, layered like sedimentary rock. Scattered across the floor are fallen door frames the size of barns, some standing on edge, others lying flat and half filled with drifted card fibre, their loose knobs resting like boulders. The storage rack closes the canyon's far end, its graphite uprights rising as broken, leaning pylons, the slots empty or jammed with shattered panels. The old floor rail runs through the drift as a buckled, pitted line. In the midground, a slim graphite gantry crane on paired rails lifts one intact door and lowers it into a rebuilt section of rack, where acid-lime alignment arms clamp the frame square. Dust haze fills the canyon.

title: File your paperwork
start: A small service counter of brushed graphite, about the size of a shoebox on its side, stands at the back centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its front has a hatch window of sandblasted frosted glass in a graphite frame, shut, with a small acid-lime bell button on the sill beside it. On the ledge in front rests one clipboard of ivory paper forms: a graphite clip holding crisp sheets with blank fields and one folded corner. Behind the glass, the soft shapes of empty filing trays are just visible. A graphite pen on a short bead chain lies across the ledge. Fine dust gathers along the window's closed seam and in the chain's links. The scene is quiet and orderly.
end: The same counter, the frosted window still shut tight, its latch unmoved. The ledge is buried: clipboards are stacked in a slumping heap, sheets fanning out and sliding off the front edge in a frozen cascade. Behind the heap, a long queue of loaded clipboards stretches back across the tabletop toward the viewer, each propped against the one before, and the rearmost are starting to topple like dominoes. A clipboard now leans on the acid-lime bell button, holding it down. The pen's bead chain has been pulled taut and snapped, loose beads frozen mid-air. Stray forms drift across the tabletop, creased flat under the weight of the queue, their corners dog-eared and grey with dust.
apocalypse: A long swell of paper dunes rolls toward a hazy horizon, each dune built of compressed forms, their edges curled and bleached, rusty-free graphite clips jutting out like rock outcrops. Among the dunes stands the service counter, now as big as a customs building, half swallowed on one side. Its frosted window is cracked in a star pattern but still shut. A line of fallen clipboards the size of billboards leads to it like a buried road. In the foreground, a slim graphite filing arm on a jointed boom reaches out from a low tracked base, lifts single forms off the dune with an acid-lime clamp and lays them into a tidy row of graphite trays set level in the sand. Grain streaks cross every slope.

title: Quota canister
start: A squat canister of sandblasted frosted glass, about the size of a jam jar, stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. It has brushed graphite end caps held by four slim rods, and a vertical graphite gauge strip down its front with a plain scale of tick marks. Inside, a thin layer of softly glowing frosted acrylic beads covers the bottom, far below a single acid-lime line marking the daily target near the top. To the left, a graphite funnel on a small stand lets one bead drop toward the open lid. To the right, an ivory card tally sheet with blank boxes is clipped to a graphite board. Fine machining scratches mark the caps, and dust sits in the rod threads.
end: The same canister is still nearly empty, its beads barely risen, the acid-lime target line high and untouched. Beside it a long row of more canisters now stretches right across the tabletop, each with its own gauge, each filled a little less than the last until the far ones are bare. The funnel has tipped over and is rolling, its last few beads bouncing mid-air across the table and missing every lid. Ivory tally sheets have multiplied and pile beneath the row, their blank boxes unchecked, some torn loose from their clips and sliding off the front edge. Scattered beads roll back toward the fallen funnel, frozen mid-bounce, and small scuffs mark where the canisters were shoved into line.
apocalypse: A dry salt flat of pale ivory crust, cracked into polygons, runs out to a flat, shimmering horizon. Across it stand dozens of giant empty canisters, each the size of a grain silo, their frosted glass dulled and chipped, graphite caps missing or tilted, rods bent. Some lie on their sides, half filled with drifted crust. A lost bead as large as a boulder rests in a crack in the foreground. At the centre, a slim graphite gantry straddles one upright canister, and a pipe from a small graphite pumping unit with an acid-lime valve wheel feeds it a steady stream of glowing frosted beads. Its refitted gauge carries a fresh acid-lime target line, and the fill has just reached it. Thin dust streaks cross the crust.

title: Production line escape
start: A compact production line of brushed graphite stretches left to right across a pale neutral tabletop, about the length of a ruler. Small ivory card cartons, crisply folded with blank labels, ride a matte belt in even spacing from a stamping press at the left toward a single square hatch at the right end, cut into a frosted acrylic wall. The hatch has a sliding graphite shutter, raised just a finger's width, with an acid-lime pull handle. A graphite crank sits idle beside the press. Behind the line, a folded ivory card apron hangs from a peg, left by whoever runs the shift. Fine card dust coats the rollers, and faint scuffs mark the belt's edges.
end: The same line has sped up: the belt is a blur, and the press at the left is kicking out cartons far faster than the hatch can pass them. At the right end the cartons have jammed against the barely open shutter, crumpling and stacking into a leaning wall that has shoved the frosted acrylic panel out of true. Behind the jam, cartons back up along the whole belt, riding over each other, and several are frozen mid-air where they have popped off the sides. The acid-lime pull handle is pinned under a crushed carton, out of reach. The crank spins loose on its axle, the apron has fallen from its peg, and flattened cartons slide off the table toward the viewer. Card dust hangs over the jam.
apocalypse: A long, collapsed factory ruin lies in a shallow valley at dawn, low light raking across it. The production line has become a long embankment of fused, crushed cartons, their ivory card grey and layered like shale, with graphite rollers poking out like broken pipes. The stamping press stands at the far end as a toppled tower, its ram snapped. The frosted acrylic wall at the near end is cracked and leaning, and beyond it opens a wide meadow of pale ivory grasses rolling to the horizon. In the foreground, a slim graphite winch rig anchored on splayed legs hauls the old hatch shutter, now tall as a barn door, upward on an acid-lime cable, while a narrow graphite ramp is being laid through the gap into the field.

title: Tunnel conformity
start: A row of seven miniature digging stations lines the front edge of a pale neutral tabletop, each a brushed graphite stand the size of a matchbox with a small shovel propped in it at exactly the same angle. The shovels have graphite blades and handles wrapped in ivory card. Behind the row, a block of pressed ivory card about the size of a brick shows seven tunnel mouths cut into its face, identical round arches at perfect intervals. One shovel near the right end has an acid-lime blade edge, fresh and unscuffed, still standing in line with the rest. Fine card dust lies in small cones below each tunnel mouth. Everything is repeated, level and exact, with no station out of place.
end: The same block has split open along its face: behind each identical mouth, identical tunnels branch in perfect copies, a honeycomb of repeated arches. But the tunnel behind the acid-lime shovel has wandered off on its own diagonal, and the block is caving in along it. A crack runs from that off-pattern tunnel across the top of the block, and slabs of pressed card are frozen mid-fall, dust pouring from the collapsing arches. The stations below are being struck: shovels are knocked from their stands and caught tumbling, and the graphite stands slide out of line. The lime-edged shovel alone stays upright, its blade dusted grey. Card crumbs scatter in a wide fan toward the viewer.
apocalypse: A soft meadow of pale ivory grass rolls toward a low horizon, its surface sunk into long collapsed troughs that trace the repeated tunnel grid below, a pattern of sagging parallel lines and round sinkholes. Through the sinkholes, cracked arches of pressed card show, packed with rubble. Enormous graphite shovel blades, weathered and pitted, jut from the turf at the same angle in a broken line, several snapped at the handle. In the midground, one sinkhole holds a slim vertical graphite shaft lift, its open cage running on acid-lime guide rails that climb straight up out of the dark toward open sky, carrying a single intact shovel on its platform. Fine fibres drift like seed heads across the grass.

title: Forms in triplicate
hero: carbon-copy form set on a clipboard
start: A graphite clipboard, about the size of a paperback, lies squarely on a pale neutral tabletop. Its clip holds a form set: a crisp ivory top sheet with blank ruled fields, then two thinner, slightly translucent copy sheets below it, separated by whisper-thin graphite carbon leaves whose edges peek out in a neat stepped fringe. An acid-lime perforation strip runs across the top of the set, where the copies are meant to tear apart. To the left, a graphite pen rests on a small stand; to the right, three shallow graphite trays wait, one for each copy. Fine fibres lift along the perforation, and faint grey smudges mark the carbon edges. Everything is square and aligned.
end: The same clipboard is now the base of a towering stack. Every form has spawned three more: sheets peel off in threes and pile upward, the stack leaning back over the clipboard far above the pen stand. The three trays are buried and overflowing, and loose carbon leaves have slipped out and fluttered down, leaving smudged grey streaks across the tabletop. Near the top, sheets are frozen mid-air, lifting and splitting apart in fans of three. The acid-lime perforation strip on the original set is still intact at the very bottom, pressed flat under the load and never torn. The clip has bent open under the weight, and the pen has been knocked from its stand and rolls toward the edge.
apocalypse: A grey-ivory tableland of compacted forms stretches to a hazy horizon, eroded into flat-topped mesas whose cliff faces show thousands of thin layered sheets, darker bands marking the pressed carbon leaves between them. At the foot of the nearest mesa lies the old clipboard, now as large as a hangar door, its clip bent upward like a broken arch. The three trays sit half buried as sunken courtyards. Loose sheets lift off the mesa tops, frozen in the wind. In the foreground, a slim graphite binding rig on four long legs has drawn one single form set out of the cliff face and clamps it inside a small graphite binder with an acid-lime spine, setting it on a clean plinth. Dust lines each ledge.

title: Files inside the computer
start: A desktop computer tower, about the height of a shoebox on end, stands at the left of a pale neutral tabletop. Its case is matte graphite metal with chamfered edges, vented side panels and four visible screws. Its front is a frosted acrylic panel with a soft internal glow and a blank drive bay. To the right, a single ivory card file folder lies flat and empty, its unmarked tab lifted. Beside the folder, a small graphite screwdriver rests unused. Through the side vents, one acid-lime drive module is faintly visible, clipped deep inside the case, holding everything anyone needs. A thin film of dust sits on top of the case, and the folder's fold is crisp.
end: The same tower has been pulled apart across the desk. Its side panel lies face down, screws scattered, and the frosted front panel has been levered off and propped against the folder, which now gapes open and still empty. Parts spread in a trail to the right: a graphite power block, a stack of fans, bent brackets, circuit boards standing on edge in frosted acrylic, and drive trays turned out and discarded. The screwdriver is caught mid-roll across a bracket, and a cover plate is frozen mid-fall off the table edge. Deep inside the gutted case, still clipped in place and untouched, the acid-lime drive module waits where nobody looked. Puffs of dust rise from the open case.
apocalypse: A wide gravel plain of graphite shards and frosted acrylic fragments stretches to a flat horizon under still air, the pieces sorted by old weather into shallow ridges. In the midground the gutted tower stands like a hollow ruined keep the size of a factory, one wall gone, its internal brackets rising as bent girders. The file folder lies nearby as a vast faded tent, collapsed and lifting at one corner, grit settled in its fold. Circuit boards stand on edge across the plain like weathered slabs. In the foreground, a slim graphite gantry has lifted the intact lime drive module out of the ruin in an acid-lime cradle and is sliding it into the reopened folder, where fresh ivory sheets are starting to stack.

title: Door falls off the car
start: A small two-door car model, about the length of a paperback, sits on a pale neutral tabletop angled to the right, parked at the start of a long strip of ivory card laid down as a road. The car's body is matte graphite metal with chamfered panels, visible rivets and scuffed bumpers, and its windows are frosted glass. On the passenger seat, visible through the open window, sits a small sample case of ivory card with graphite corners, lid shut. The driver's door hangs a fraction low, its acid-lime hinge pin already backing out of its socket. A folded ivory road map lies on the dashboard. Fine grit sits along the road strip, and dust dulls the hubcaps.
end: The same car has driven on down the ivory card road and is now far to the right, still moving, its wheels blurred. Behind it, the driver's door lies flat on the road where it fell, the acid-lime hinge pin frozen mid-bounce beside it. Through the open side, the sample case has slid off the seat and burst: small ivory card sample boxes and graphite sample tins spill in a long trail back along the road, some frozen mid-tumble, some split and scattering tiny frosted acrylic samples. The folded map has blown out of the window and hangs mid-air, half unfolded. Scuff marks and a thin line of grit trace from the car all the way back to the fallen door.
apocalypse: A long desert highway of cracked ivory card runs to a vanishing point between low mesas of faded grit. Its shoulders are strewn with weathered sample boxes the size of sheds, split open, their contents drifted into sand. The fallen car door lies across the road like a toppled billboard, its graphite panel pitted and bleached pale. Far down the road sits the car itself, now as large as a house, wheels sunk to the hubs, frosted windows crazed, the sample case a sagging ruin on its seat. In the foreground, a slim graphite tow rig on four independent wheels has hooked the car with an acid-lime tow hitch and a taut graphite cable and is dragging it back toward the door, leaving two neat tracks.

title: Cold-call phone bank
start: A single desk telephone, about the size of a paperback, sits on a bare graphite desk at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, with wide empty space around it suggesting a large open floor. The phone has a matte graphite body, a frosted acrylic keypad with blank keys and a handset resting in its cradle on a neat coiled cord. A small acid-lime indicator lamp on its face is lit, marking one incoming line. Beside it lies an ivory card call sheet with blank ruled lines and a graphite pen. An empty graphite chair is pushed back from the desk, a folded ivory card jacket draped over it. Fine dust sits in the keypad grooves, and the cord shows slight wear.
end: The same desk is now one of many. Phones have multiplied across the tabletop into a crowded trading floor: handsets on every surface, stacked two and three high on desks, piled on chairs, lined up along the floor between them. Every handset has jolted out of its cradle and hangs frozen a finger's width above it, cords stretched. Call sheets have slid off the desks in drifts. The original phone at the centre is buried under a heap of others, only its acid-lime lamp still glowing through the pile. The empty chair has rolled backward and tipped, its jacket sliding off. Rattling handsets have walked across the desks, leaving scuffs, and dust shakes loose in fine clouds.
apocalypse: A vast, silent flatland of dead handsets stretches to a hazy horizon, each one the size of a car, bleached and cracked, receivers lying off their cradles and half sunk in a floor of drifted, yellowed call sheets. Coiled cords as thick as tree trunks lie slack and snapped between them. Frosted keypads lie scattered like broken tiles. In the middle distance, the original desk rises as a weathered platform on bent graphite legs, its phone a slumped mound. Nothing is ringing. In the foreground, a slim graphite line-laying rig on a narrow wheeled chassis unspools a single acid-lime cable across the plain, running from one handset it has lifted and set upright back to the old desk.

title: Save the shop
start: A small shop counter of brushed graphite, about the size of a shoebox, stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its frosted glass display front softly glowing from within. On top sits a compact till: a graphite body, blank frosted acrylic keys and a closed cash drawer. Beside the till, one ivory envelope with a blank label leans against a small graphite bell, its flap closed with an acid-lime seal that marks it as the rent notice. Behind the counter, a short graphite shelf holds a few ivory card boxes of stock. A folded ivory apron hangs from a hook at one end of the counter. Light dust lies along the till's keys and the shelf edge.
end: The same counter is sinking. Plain-sealed ivory envelopes have piled onto it in a slumping mound that buries the till up to its keys and spills over both ends. The counter's graphite legs have buckled, and it sags into the tabletop at one corner, the frosted display front cracked diagonally. Envelopes are frozen mid-slide off the mound, fanning out across the floor toward the viewer. The cash drawer has sprung open, empty. The original envelope with the acid-lime seal sits near the bottom of the pile, pressed flat. The stock shelf behind leans forward, one box caught mid-fall. The bell lies on its side, and the apron has slipped from its hook.
apocalypse: A low hill of weathered ivory envelopes rolls away to a quiet horizon, layered and fused into pale strata like old snowpack. At its heart sits the shop, now the size of a small building, sunk to its roofline: the graphite counter is a cracked lintel and the till a slumped boulder of blank keys. A graphite roller shutter, pitted and dented, has come down across the whole front. In the foreground, a slim graphite unlocking rig on a jointed arm reaches up and turns an acid-lime key in the shutter's lock, while a pair of graphite winches on either side have started to lift the shutter, revealing a strip of soft frosted light from inside. Loose envelopes slide down the slopes.

title: Box on the way out
hero: ivory card box of desk belongings
start: An empty ivory card box, about the size of a shoebox, sits open at the centre of a pale graphite desk on a neutral tabletop, its flaps folded out and creased crisp. Around it the desk is still set up: a frosted glass mug, a small graphite desk lamp, a framed ivory card photo turned away with a blank back, and a graphite stapler. In front of the box lies a studio access badge, a frosted acrylic card with a blank face, on a neatly coiled acid-lime lanyard. Behind the desk, a long corridor begins as a strip of pale floor running away between low graphite walls. Dust sits in the stapler's hinge, and the box corners show faint scuffs.
end: The same box is now packed and overfull, its flaps forced upright: the mug, the lamp with its cord trailing out, the stapler and the frame are jammed inside at angles. It rides on a slim graphite hand trolley rolling away down the long corridor, frozen mid-motion, wheels blurred and leaving a thin scuff line. Behind it, the stripped desk shows only pale rectangles in the dust where things stood. The frame has slipped from the box and is caught mid-fall, and loose ivory papers flutter out in its wake. The acid-lime lanyard hangs over the box's edge, the badge swinging out on it. The corridor's graphite walls recede in a long, even line.
apocalypse: A long, dim hall of studio ruins stretches away, its roof long gone and the sky pale overhead. Tall graphite lighting gantries stand bent and half fallen, and sheets of ivory card backdrop hang torn from their frames in deep folds. The floor is a drift of dust and fallen flats, and the old corridor runs through it as a cracked causeway. At its far end sits the box, now the size of a cottage, weathered and sagging, flaps curled open, the lamp's shade jutting out like a chimney. From a slim graphite tripod crane in the foreground, an acid-lime spotlight throws a clean circle of light onto the box, while the crane's graphite hook lowers toward it to lift it free.

title: Temp supply mystery
start: A graphite supply shelf, about the height of a cereal box, stands at the right of a pale neutral tabletop, its three levels neatly stocked with ivory card notepads, a row of graphite staplers, tape in frosted acrylic dispensers and small boxes of clips. At the left sits a small graphite temp desk, bare except for a single ivory pad and a frosted acrylic visitor badge on an acid-lime clip. A graphite desk lamp is angled down onto the pad. Between the shelf and the temp desk stand two taller graphite desks with shallow drawers, closed. The shelf edges are clean where items were recently straightened, and dust lies only in the back corners.
end: The same supply shelf is half empty, pale dust-free rectangles marking where staplers and pads have vanished, and a few stragglers are frozen mid-slide off the edge. On the two taller desks, the drawers have slammed shut and small graphite padlocks hang from them, still swinging. Every desk lamp in the scene has swivelled on its arm to point at the temp desk, which sits in a hard pool of overlapping light, the acid-lime badge clip glaring in it. Its single pad has been knocked askew. A trail of paper clips runs across the tabletop from the shelf, not to the temp desk, but into the gap behind one locked drawer.
apocalypse: A long warehouse aisle runs to a vanishing point, lined on both sides with toppled graphite shelving the size of apartment blocks, their levels bare and furred with grey-ivory dust that has settled into rippled drifts across the floor. Desk lamps as tall as streetlights lean over the aisle, shades cracked. The small temp desk stands intact beneath them, its badge long faded. In the midground, a slim graphite inventory rig rolls down the centre on a single rail, sweeping an acid-lime scanning bar across the shelves. It has stopped beside a buried desk drawer the size of a shipping container, now pried open to reveal a neat hidden stash of staplers, pads and clips. Dust eddies in the rig's wake.

title: Plaque race
start: A long miniature store aisle runs away from the viewer down the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, flanked by two low graphite shelving units stocked with neat rows of ivory card boxes and frosted acrylic jars. At the far end, on a graphite end wall, hangs one empty plaque frame, a rectangle of brushed graphite with an acid-lime backing card and nothing mounted on it. A single graphite wire shopping cart, about the size of a matchbox, is parked at the near end pointing down the aisle. The floor tiles carry faint scuffs. The shelves are faced perfectly, and a fine line of dust runs along the lowest shelf lip.
end: The same aisle has become a racetrack. Several graphite carts are frozen mid-charge down it, wheels blurred and splayed, one tipped onto two wheels, another rammed into a shelf. Their wakes have swept stock off both sides: ivory boxes tumble in mid-air, jars roll and bounce, and one shelf leans inward, shedding its contents in a slide. At the end wall, the acid-lime frame is now surrounded by a spreading grid of more empty plain graphite frames, crowding up and outward toward the ceiling, several hanging crooked. Skid marks on the floor tiles run straight back to the near end of the aisle, where the first cart stood.
apocalypse: A long canyon of collapsed shelving stretches toward a pale horizon, the shelves now as big as office towers, fallen inward against each other to form a jagged arch overhead. The floor is a sediment of crushed ivory boxes and frosted acrylic fragments drifted into banks. Dented graphite carts the size of trucks lie on their sides, wheels in the air, half buried. The end wall still stands far off, its grid of empty frames hanging askew and bleached. In the foreground, one slim graphite cart rig with acid-lime wheels rolls clear of the debris along a newly laid graphite track, carrying the original plaque frame upright on its bed, its backing faded. Dust settles slowly behind it.

title: Pudding loophole
start: A single dessert cup, about the size of a shot glass, stands on a brushed graphite stockroom shelf that runs across the back of a pale neutral tabletop. The cup is frosted acrylic with a milky glow, sealed with a crisp ivory paper lid pressed flat at the rim. Beside it, clipped to the shelf edge by a small graphite clip, hangs one coupon of ivory card with deckled perforated edges, a blank face and a thin acid-lime stripe along its top border. The rest of the shelf is empty. Below, a folded ivory delivery slip and a graphite box cutter lie on the tabletop. Fine dust sits along the shelf lip.
end: The same shelf now sags under towers of identical frosted cups, stacked in pyramids and columns up to the top of the frame. The shelf has bowed in the middle, and cups slide off it in a frozen cascade, rolling across the tabletop in a flood that pours toward the front edge, out toward unseen warehouse aisles. The coupon hangs at a steep angle from its clip, its acid-lime stripe still visible, and a long ribbon of plain clipped coupons now trails from it down to the floor. Delivery slips have piled into a drift, and several paper lids have popped off and hang mid-air. The box cutter is buried under the cups.
apocalypse: A vast warehouse ruin opens under a broken graphite roof, pale sky showing through the gaps. Its floor has become dunes of frosted cups, each now the size of a car, drifted in rippling banks against toppled racking, lids peeled and bleached, some cracked and filled with pale grit. The old aisles show as troughs between the dunes, running to a hazy back wall. The stockroom shelf juts out of the nearest dune as a bent girder, its faded coupon still clipped on. In the foreground, a low, slim graphite pallet rig with acid-lime forks pulls out from under a dune, carrying one tidy pallet of cups stacked square and strapped with ivory card bands along a cleared lane toward an open loading door.

title: Honesty in the meeting
start: A polished oval meeting table of brushed graphite, about the size of a serving tray, fills the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its surface softly reflecting the light. Six small graphite chairs are tucked in evenly around it. At the head of the table lies one ivory agenda sheet, crisp and square with blank lines, and on it rests a slim graphite pen with an acid-lime cap. In the middle stands a frosted glass water carafe with six empty frosted glasses. A folded ivory card name tent with a blank face sits at each seat. The polish shows only one tiny scuff near the head of the table, and a faint dust haze lies on the chair backs.
end: The same table has been jolted. The agenda sheet is torn cleanly across the middle, the two halves lifting apart in mid-air, and the acid-lime-capped pen is frozen mid-spin above the tear. From the head of the table, the disruption runs outward: name tents have flipped and slide off the edges, the carafe has tipped and its water arcs out in a sheet across the table, glasses topple in a chain, and papers skid toward the far end. Chairs have rolled back on their casters, some turned sideways, one tipping over backward. Water droplets and paper corners trace a clear line back to the torn agenda at the head.
apocalypse: A wide, dim plain of cracked polished stone stretches to a low horizon, and across it lies the meeting table, now the size of a runway, split lengthwise into two tilted slabs with a deep ravine between them. Old water has dried into pale rings on its surface. The chairs, big as houses, lie scattered and overturned, casters in the air, some half buried in drifts of torn ivory paper. The frosted carafe lies shattered in a fan of fragments. In the foreground, a slim graphite lifting rig running on paired rails has righted one chair at the head of the split table and braces it upright with acid-lime struts, set square to the table's end. Fine grit drifts across the slabs.

title: Eight-to-noon window
start: A round wall clock, about the size of a saucer, hangs on a pale graphite wall panel at the upper left of the frame. It has a brushed graphite rim, a frosted glass face with a plain dial with tick marks, slim graphite hands, and a thin acid-lime arc painted along one third of the dial, marking the promised service window. To the right, a small front door of ivory card with a graphite knob stands closed in a graphite frame. Below the clock, one ivory card chair waits beside the door, a folded jacket over its back and a cold frosted mug on the floor beside it. Dust sits along the threshold. The hands rest just inside the start of the arc.
end: The same clock now shows its hands swept far past the acid-lime arc, the minute hand frozen mid-blur as it spins around again. The front door is still shut, its knob untouched and dusty. Where one chair stood, a long queue of identical ivory card chairs stretches from the door down a hallway that recedes toward the back of the frame, each with a cold mug beside it, the nearest chairs tipping as the line compresses. The folded jacket has slipped to the floor. Loose blank ivory pages have slid off one seat and fan out in mid-air. A trail of knocked-over mugs leads back along the queue to the door.
apocalypse: A long, roofless hallway runs to a distant point, its graphite walls cracked and leaning, the floor carpeted with drifts of pale dust and fallen ivory card. Chairs the size of cottages line both sides in a broken queue, many tipped over, some half sunk. Across the hallway lies the wall clock, now enormous, fallen flat on its back like a crater rim, its frosted face shattered and its hands bent upward, the old painted arc faded to grey. At the hallway's end stands the front door, tall as a tower. In the foreground, a slim graphite winch rig on tracks has fixed an acid-lime cable to the door's knob and is hauling it open, a wedge of clean light falling across the dust.

title: Auto-layoff machine
start: A row of five small office desks, each about the size of a matchbox, lines up across a pale neutral tabletop on a pair of slim graphite rails set flush into the surface. Each desk is brushed graphite with an ivory card top, a tidy stack of ivory papers and a pushed-in chair. On each desk sits a slim graphite evaluation box the size of a sugar cube, with a frosted acrylic window and a small flag arm folded down. Only the box on the middle desk has its acid-lime flag arm lifted, halfway up. At the right end of the rails, a short graphite ramp slopes down to the table edge. Fine dust lies in the rail grooves.
end: The same row is mid-ejection. The evaluation boxes are flagging desks automatically, flag arms rising one after another, and flagged desks are frozen shooting sideways along the rails, papers lifting off their tops in sheets, chairs tipping backward off them. The middle desk with the acid-lime flag leads the way, already launched off the ramp and caught in mid-air past the table edge, its box still attached. Two more desks follow close behind, grinding on the rails in bursts of metal dust. Gaps open in the row where desks stood, and the remaining boxes are just raising their plain graphite flags. Papers drift in a trail back along the rails.
apocalypse: A wide plain of dry ivory grass spreads under a pale horizon, scattered with ejected desks the size of houses lying where they landed: upturned, sunk on one corner, split open with papers spilling into the grass. Deep gouges run from each desk back toward the centre, where a burnt-out evaluation box, now the size of a control bunker, sits scorched dull grey, its frosted window cracked and its flag arms seized. The old rails radiate outward, bent and broken. In the midground, a slim graphite rail-laying rig with acid-lime tongs has placed one fresh straight pair of rails and is setting a single desk back onto them, square and level, the start of a restored row.

title: Stock goes to zero
start: A round desk gauge, about the size of a saucer, stands on a short graphite pedestal at the centre of a large brushed graphite executive desk on a pale neutral tabletop. It has a frosted glass face with a plain dial with tick marks and a slim acid-lime needle pointing high toward the right of the scale. Around it the office is fully furnished in miniature: a tall-backed chair, a graphite floor lamp glowing through a frosted acrylic shade, a low cabinet of ivory card files, and a framed blank ivory picture on the wall behind. A folded unprinted ivory paper lies beside the gauge. Everything is polished, settled and dust-free.
end: The same gauge now shows its acid-lime needle dropped hard to the far left, frozen mid-bounce against the stop. Around it the office is being emptied in motion: the chair rolls away backward toward the right edge, the cabinet has been tipped onto a graphite dolly with files spilling from open drawers, and the frame on the wall has come down and is caught mid-fall. The floor lamp is switched off, its frosted shade dark. A second lamp is already gone, leaving a pale ring in fresh dust on the floor. Loose ivory files drift across the desk, now bare except for the gauge and the folded paper, and scrape marks trail toward the door.
apocalypse: A vast empty office ruin opens into a dim plateau, its walls fallen outward to leave only a floor slab of cracked graphite panels stretching to the horizon, marked with pale ghost rectangles where furniture once stood. Drifts of ivory files have blown into the corners and lie in wind-shaped banks. Near the centre, the executive desk has collapsed onto one side, and the gauge lies on the floor beside it, now as big as a satellite dish, its frosted face crazed and its old needle bent flat at the bottom of the scale. A slim graphite tripod rig stands over it and, with a fine acid-lime lever arm, lifts a new needle off the stop, just starting to rise. Dust sifts across the floor.

title: Unpaid internship
start: A plain bus stop shelter of brushed graphite and frosted glass, about the height of a mug, stands at the left of a pale neutral tabletop. Under its bench, a slim ivory card briefcase with graphite clasps rests upright beside a heavy equipment case: a squat graphite box the size of a matchbox with chamfered corners, a stout carrying handle and an acid-lime latch. To the right, a thin strip of ivory card road runs off toward a small cluster of graphite buildings in the background. A folded ivory card jacket lies across the bench. The case has pressed a small dent into the tabletop beneath it, and dust sits along its seams.
end: The same road now stretches across the whole tabletop, looping and winding past a long line of identical bus stop shelters receding into the distance. At each stop the equipment case sits a little bigger and heavier than at the last, and the final one has grown as large as the shelter itself, crushing the bench flat, cracking the frosted glass and sinking into the tabletop in a spray of chips frozen mid-air. The acid-lime latch sits on that last case, straining at its hinge. The briefcase lies toppled and open at one of the middle stops, papers sliding out. Deep drag marks run along the road from stop to stop, back to the first shelter.
apocalypse: A dim city ruin climbs a long hillside at dusk, its graphite buildings roofless and gapped, the streets choked with pale drift and fallen ivory card. The winding road from before is visible as a cracked switchback terraced up the slope, lined with the bent frames of bus shelters. At the foot of the hill sits the equipment case, as big as a warehouse, its handle arching overhead like a bridge, its corners dented and dusty, its latch faded. In the midground, a slim graphite funicular tram on a single steep rail has taken a small intact equipment case aboard its flat car and climbs toward the hilltop, drawn by an acid-lime cable wheel at the summit station.

title: Wiped project memory
start: A small ivory paper envelope, about the size of a playing card, lies open at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its flap unfolded along crisp creases. Laid out in a neat row beside it are its contents: a graphite key, a folded ivory ticket stub with a blank face, a frosted acrylic marble, a small graphite paperclip, a blank ivory card, and a thin acid-lime thread wound around a graphite spool. Behind the row sit an empty graphite desk organiser and a cold frosted mug, left by someone who is not coming back to explain. Nothing shows why these objects belong together. Fibres fray at the envelope's edges, and dust lies in the key's teeth.
end: The same desk is now crowded with unexplained objects. More items have spilled from the envelope, which lies torn and empty: graphite washers, frosted marbles, ivory card squares, small bolts and more keys have multiplied across the tabletop in loose clusters. Between them, dozens of blank ivory sticky notes cling to everything, curling at the corners, many frozen mid-fall as they peel away. The desk organiser has tipped over, spilling still more. The marble from the original row is caught rolling off the front edge. Only the spool of acid-lime thread sits where it was, its loose end trailing a short way across the table toward the key. Dust hangs in the air above the clutter.
apocalypse: A dim basin of scattered objects spreads toward a low, misty horizon, each item now the size of a building and half sunk in pale dust. A graphite key lies like a fallen bridge, frosted marbles rest as cloudy domes, washers stand on edge like ruined arches, and blank ivory cards jut from the ground as tilted slabs. Faded notes cover the ground like leaf litter, and the torn envelope forms a collapsed ridge in the background. In the foreground, a slim graphite survey rig on a long tracked chassis drives acid-lime stakes beside each object and draws a single taut acid-lime line between them, linking the key, then a marble, then a card, in order.

title: Erase the bad project
inspired_by: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004)
start: A thick project folder of ivory card, about the size of a paperback, lies closed at the centre of a pale graphite desk on a neutral tabletop, its unmarked tab lifting slightly and its spine creased from use. A graphite desk lamp with a frosted acrylic shade bends over it, casting a soft pool of light. Beside the folder, a single acid-lime paper clip holds a small bundle of loose ivory sheets. Around the desk, the corner of a miniature room is visible: a graphite shelf of ivory binders, a sandblasted frosted glass window and a chair pushed back with a cardigan draped over it. A scatter of pale eraser crumbs lies beside the folder.
end: The same desk sits under the same lamp, but the room is being erased from its edges inward. The far walls, the window and the shelf are breaking apart into pale grains that drift off in mid-air, their outlines softening into haze. The binders on the shelf are half gone, cut off mid-spine. The chair has lost its back legs and is tilting, the cardigan sliding off. The desk's own edges are fraying into dust. At the centre, the folder lies open and its pages lift out one by one, each dissolving into ivory flecks as it rises. The acid-lime clip has sprung open, and the loose sheets beneath it are fading first.
apocalypse: A wide, pale plain stretches to a horizon that simply fades out, and across it lie the ruins of the room, enormous and incomplete. A graphite shelf is missing half its length, cut clean where it ends in nothing. The lamp is bent over, tall as a crane, its frosted shade crumbled away. The desk is broken in half, its far edge fraying into drifting grains. Pale dunes of fine erased dust fill the gaps between them. In the foreground, a slim graphite plotting gantry on four long legs traces an acid-lime outline across the ground through a fine graphite nozzle, redrawing the room's original floor edge, while behind it the first wall panel is lifted back into place along the line.
